rationale: Speaker says he can operate an alien educator without understanding it; nothing about decoding thoughts or images, so no match to the fMRI reconstruction.
A wristband starting a helicopter points to a worn token granting machine access, but the 1961 milestone is a card inserted to log time and attendance.
Glowing colored sparks marking ships in space loosely suggest a spatial display, but nothing says it is volumetric or viewable from several sides as in the Perspecta.
A mind-probe used on trials is the right sort of device, but the quotation only says it was deceived and describes no decoding of imagery from brain activity.
Specialized robot servants that shove aside obstacles gesture at service robots, but the quote gives no taking of orders or waiting on diners.
Pass cards fed into a slot at an automatic gate guard match machines reading cards to grant entry; the 1961 case was attendance logging, a different context.
A wristband pressed to a lock-face to identify the wearer matches a worn token read by a machine for identity; the milestone is a card inserted for attendance.
The quoted lines describe only a man's expression changing from belligerent to astonished and say nothing about scanning an eye.
A robot guiding technologists to records and following simple directions points toward record retrieval, but there is no query matching against a stored collection.
Screens that turn the subconscious into pictures evoke displaying dreams, but fMRI decoding of imagined visual patterns is a far narrower, mechanistically different feat.
A giant machine finding a matching picture in its files with all details in seconds fits fast record retrieval; the match is by image, not a typed query.
The quote only describes a fat man in dark glasses and the respect of others; nothing about identifying someone by voice.
A vault lock keyed to a single chosen thought is an access control, but it is not a card or token read for identity and nothing reads thoughts as in the milestone.
A helmet gathering thought vibrations via a diaphragm and wiring them onward is a crude mind-reading idea, but it claims no decoding of specific images as the fMRI work did.
A metal ident card tripping relays at a gate to pass a person matches a card machines read to grant access; the robot guards add context beyond the 1961 attendance use.
Demanding a court order before police read a suspect's memory concerns legal access to a memory-reading procedure, but gives no mechanism approximating the fMRI decoding.
A chart projection screen showing the fleet's position in space matches a screen displaying tracked object positions; SAGE used live radar data and consoles.
A device that implants knowledge into a sleeper is a learning machine; the milestone is only playing word pairs during slow-wave sleep, and the quote's mind-reading part is not the match.
A dial-and-light controlled bartender fetching brandy and soda loosely evokes a serving robot, but it takes no order from diners as the 1985 waiters did.
Locking ship machinery to open only to one person's characteristic motions is identity-based access control, but it is not a card or token.
A thinkwriter that lets a reporter compose text suggests thought-to-text, but the quote says nothing of reading brain activity or visual patterns.
A book-screen the reader looks up from matches a portable screen displaying electronic books; the quote gives no detail on portability or storage.
A keyless typewriter-shaped machine replacing a secretary matches automatic dictation; the quote does not say it recognizes words, and the summary says waveform on paper.
A brain recorder feeding a device that projects a captive's thoughts as three-dimensional pictures matches thought display in function; fMRI reconstruction was only of simple visual patterns.
Voice-ordered deletion of records points to spoken commands to a computer, but the quote describes erasure with no recognizing of words as in the VIP-100.
A battered voicewriter in an office names a voice-driven writing machine but the quote says nothing of how it works or transcribes.
Robot salesmen built to think like humans describe a design theory for artificial personalities, not machines serving customers as waiters or clerks.
A central intelligence over robots is mentioned, but the quote only gives its beliefs about mass and energy, not coordinating carriers as at Kalmar.
Robot-proctor guards over workmen loosely resemble security robots, but the quote gives no patrolling or credential checking.
A robot set to search for people by profession and class fits finding records matching a query; the dictation to a steno-robot adds context.
A cardex chewing on evidence implies an index machine reasoning over detector data, but the quotation says nothing about finding matching items from stored records.
A computer matching measured crystal properties against memory banks to identify a compound fits database search by attributes; it is not a document query by terminal.
A computer-clerk displaying a layout on a panel hints at a reception machine, but it is a stationary display rather than a robot serving the public.
A giant map mirroring live activity in strategic cities fits a computer-driven situation display; SAGE showed radar tracks, not city activity.
A Great Brain charged with a civilization's knowledge points to a knowledge store, but the quote includes no answering of questions in ordinary language.
A ship's computer taking spoken orders to plot a course fits voice commands; the milestone was isolated-word industrial recognition.
A central records archive projected instantly to offices matches remote retrieval of records; the milestone is a telephone terminal for search.
Taking a retinal pattern and checking it against an identity center's records matches retinal identification; the 1984 scanner used it for access control.
A library view-screen with index buttons to read text from tapes matches quick retrieval of stored documents; the quote shows no query search.
A robot clerk's camera recording a traveler's face for later police use matches face capture; it does not describe matching against stored images.
An electronic scanner guard passing a person by identification matches credential-checking security machines; the 1986 Sentry was a patrolling robot.
Cameras whose pictures are linked to an ident-card at a police bureau suggest identity matching, but the quote does not say the card is read to grant access.
Thousands of ships tied by robot controls to act in coordination hint at centralized control, but the quote names no single computer directing it.
A service record on a strip of stereofac paper is only a printout delivered to a drawer; the quote says nothing about searching a collection.
A master computer the size of a refrigerator that answers questions suggests a Q&A machine, but the quote gives no language input or breadth of knowledge.
Children taught directly from the Brain's informational resources suggests a central knowledge store feeding students, not a computer directing a robot fleet.
Converting a person's thought into an electron flow that drives a robot's voice is a thought-to-speech idea, but fMRI decoding of imagined visual patterns is a different mechanism and output.
A robot dealer running a casino game gestures at robots serving the public, but the milestone was robot waiters taking dinner orders; the quote is about a spinning light device.
Hunting reference tapes and coming up with exactly the information needed matches finding relevant stored records; no query or telephone terminal is described.
A robot operator answering and connecting a call with priority is a receptionist-like role, but it is switchboard service, not serving customers in person.
A wire touch that records thoughts is a crude contact mind-reader, but no decoding of imagined visuals or specific thoughts is described.
An ambulance computer relaying limited ideas hints at thought translation, but the quotation does not show a device writing thoughts as text or images.
A machine registering a brain-wave signature stored on a cylinder is a biometric recording, not a card or token encoded with identity read to grant access.
The quote only says a case opened wide on the floor; the voice-activation lies in the summary, not the quotation, so any link to speech recognition is faint.
Robot guardians whose orders cannot be changed or bribed point at security robots, but no patrolling or checking of credentials is stated.
Slipping a photo into a slot and pressing Search to find a person's file matches automatic retrieval of a matching record; it is image-based rather than a typed query.
A thought-screen recording audiences' brain impulses and synthesizing them is a mind-reading display, but a composite of crowd reactions differs from decoding a specific imagined image.
A robot that, when prompted, slides open a stomach panel to give two drinks matches a bartending machine serving customers; the milestone was robot waiters at a restaurant.
The quote says only that Ned shot the answer back; the summary's record matching is not in the quotation, so the match is weak.
A punch-card robot attending the check-in desk fits a robot clerk or receptionist serving the public; the 1985 waiters were mobile and took food orders.
A belt device reading another's thoughts word for word matches mind-reading in function, though the mechanism is unstated and far beyond fMRI reconstruction of simple patterns.
Plastic robots acting under World Brain to carry out its functions match one master computer directing many robots; Kalmar's carriers were guided but not humanoid.
A robot taking baggage claim checks at a hotel desk matches a robot clerk serving guests; the milestone was restaurant waiters.
An electronic cross-index of a library hints at indexed retrieval, but this quote says nothing about the machine finding items in seconds.
Switching a stenoreel to transcriber mode matches turning recorded dictation into text; it does not say recognition by word, as the Kurzweil system did.
Sound analyzers that cannot be fooled by an imitated living voice match voice-based authentication of a person; the starship context differs from a computer center's access control.
A remote hypnosis beam reading innermost thoughts is a mind-reading device but at a distance and with no decoding mechanism comparable to fMRI classifiers.
A mathematically exact translation of oral sound by a dictation typewriter matches speech-to-text; the 1986 systems used limited vocabularies and the quote is silent on mechanism.
A secretary transcribing conversation on an audioscriber suggests a dictation machine; the quote leaves unclear whether the machine itself produces text.
A machine used to learn a human's language, thoughts and name matches reading a mind; the quote gives no mechanism, and fMRI decoding recovered only imagined visual patterns.
A guard robot on the ground floor bleeping an alert matches a building security robot signaling; patrolling is not mentioned.
A robot operator answering that the pilot is unavailable loosely points to service robots, but it serves no public customer as a waiter or clerk.
A machine-check of colonists' personal attributes was a dropped plan, with no sign of storing or querying records.
The quote says only that a facility is the largest in the world; any central brain directing artificial persons comes from the summary, not the text.
The cross-index with a voice interface is in the summary but the quote only names an electronic cross-index, so spoken commands are not shown.
A probe that would save time over taped debriefing suggests extracting an agent's memories directly; no mechanism is given and fMRI work recovered only imagined visual patterns.
A keyboard and screen on a desk wall tied to a central filing system match querying a remote record store via a terminal; the 1967 terminal used telephone lines.
Vocowriters among equipment supplied imply speech-to-text devices, but the quotation only names them without detail.
A psycho-search that screens brain patterns and is fooled by a false one suggests mind-reading screening, with no actual decoding of thoughts.
A director voicing a request into a mouthpiece for a statistical summary matches spoken input to a computer; the quote concerns data retrieval more than recognizing words.
A cap that reads all thoughts and stops lying matches a head-worn mind-reading device in function; no mechanism is given.
A tiny temple electrode wired to a pocket device points to head-sensing, but the quote says only it monitors, not that it reads thoughts or images.
Detectors that catch thought patterns for identifying and filing individuals evoke brain-pattern recognition, not decoding of specific thoughts or images.
Robot guards wired to a central desk that alarms on abnormal performance is remote monitoring of robots; the Sentry patrolled autonomously and the quote describes no credential checks.
Reading Nalboon's ideas from a dead officer's brain matches pulling specific thoughts from a brain; no instrument or method is described.
Manufactured mechanical wives with memory tapes as minds are companion robots, but the Furby is a toy with no romantic function.
An information machine dispensing a map of Level 10 matches getting a requested item from a stored collection; the milestone is a remote search terminal.
Punching a designation on a keyboard and instantly seeing it on a screen matches a terminal that retrieves stored records; the 1967 system was remote by telephone.
The quote shows a man cursing and hoping he committed himself to nothing; nothing about eyes or scanning.
An autoscanner on a radar-like device ready to sound at the first blip on screens matches computer-assisted detection display; the quote describes an alarm more than tracks shown.
A machine-reporter of thoughts and feelings is a title only, naming a recorder of a council with no sign of speech transcription.
The computer housed in Central Control as the brain and nerves of the station matches a computer running a station's functions; Skylab's computer handled attitude control, a narrower role.
A three-dimensional map hanging in mid-air as if glued to nothing matches a volumetric map display in function; the Perspecta was a spinning-screen display used for medical planning.
Turning each thought vibration into a distinct quality of light is an early idea of displaying thought, but it yields colors for a spectroscope, not text or images of mental content.
A librarian submitting foreign literature to idea-content analysis suggests machine analysis of documents, but it describes no retrieval of items matching a query.
An auto-receptionist in offices matches a robot receptionist serving visitors; the quote says only that nobody needs more, with no detail of operation.
Making a quick tape on the cyb hints at a machine consulted for records, but the quote gives only a vague act of recording, not a search for items.
A brain-machine controlled by thoughts is a thought-control interface; it does not describe one computer directing many robots as in Kalmar.
Feeding a new repair circuit into the central computer so robots act on it matches a central computer controlling many robots; Kalmar's central guidance was routing carriers.
Filaments glowing with the ship's pulse show live status of mechanisms, which is a status display, not positions of tracked objects as on SAGE consoles.
A robot taken to a destination by spoken command matches voice commands carried out by a machine; the formulaic order adds context and recognition is unspecified.

Thought turned into vision or expression for everyone to read matches displaying a person's thoughts as text or pictures; the mechanism is vague and fMRI work reconstructed only simple imagined patterns.
A spool askew in a thinkwriter implies a recording device, but the quotation says nothing about listening to dictation or producing text.
A big telechart plate used for interstellar navigation matches a screen showing positions of nearby objects; live tracking from sensors is not stated in the quote.
People learning the visitors' story while they lay unconscious implies knowledge taken from memory, but no device or decoded content is described.
A seven-hundred-foot operations tank implies a giant battle plotting display; the quote gives only size, and SAGE showed live radar tracks on consoles.
A Hypno-Mech Tape Library matches recorded lessons played during hypnosis; the quote is a title with no sleep or details on the lessons.
Dialing a library and asking a robot for information fits a robot librarian serving a patron remotely; the 1985 waiters served diners in person.
Navy robots pouring coffee for spacemen match robot servants serving drinks, close to the Tanbo waiters; the quote is only a complaint about hot coffee.
Cruiser-finders tuned to detect air-city motors are detectors; the quote does not describe a computer display of positions.
Dialing a library and asking the robot for information on the Institute fits remote retrieval of a requested item; no search speed or storage is described.
Machines that probe a man's inner thoughts to catch spies describe mind-reading in function, but nothing on reading specific images and the vague mechanism.
A gliding robot redcap suggests a porter, but it is carrying luggage rather than taking orders or serving customers by speech.
Taking a helmet and scanning someone suggests a head-worn brain scanner, but it does not say anything is read.
A giant metal creature built to kill is a guardian robot, but it has no patrol or credential checking as in the Sentry.
A secretary with contact-buttons at her temples operating a Mento-Writer matches writing thoughts as text via head electrodes; fMRI decoded imagined visual patterns, not text.
Calls for electrograph and viewplate records on varied subjects from all over the city match remote on-demand retrieval of stored records.
A ring applied to a photoelectric mechanism to open a hangar matches a token read by a machine for access; the 1961 card logged attendance.
A door that opens when told 'Regan' and an elevator that does not answer match voice commands, with the elevator failing; the quote shows speaker-specific name use.
A mind stuffed with ragged bits of information has no display in the quote, so the summary's reader-viewer is unsupported.
A line dictated for a letter, accepted, matches voice dictation producing letters; the quote gives no machine action.
A robot unable to connect a changed voice to the one it knows matches machine recognition of a voice; it shows the weakness of voice-based identification.
Nozzles oozing plastic that build up a scanned shape match additive fabrication from a form; the milestone used a laser-cured resin from a digital design.
A plan to fake computation results to deceive the public says nothing of a machine answering factual questions.
A man sleep-learning the Martian language on a hop matches the sleep-learning idea, but the quote lacks any recorded lessons and the 2019 results were only word-pair associations.
Plugging in a machine and playing a reel of a father's voice to teach a sleeper fits playing recorded lessons during sleep; the 2019 study used word pairs.
Cybing for someone's master file after an arrest report matches retrieving a person's record from a computer system on request.
Colored points of light marking a ship and other bodies match a display plotting live positions; the system is not computer-run in the quote.
A galactic atlas queried by buttons that returns survey data matches a stored collection answering queries; the milestone was a text terminal.
Central File as an intelligence directing robots to kill is only referenced as an unspecific database, so the match to a fleet of guided carriers is loose.
Serving-robots doing a rush business in hot coffee evoke robot servers, but aboard a warship for the crew rather than serving the public.
Feeding a photo into a tracer for an unlimited file search for resembling persons matches image-based search through an archive for faces; early systems were limited to a few thousand images.
Collecting thought's invisible vibrations is a detection claim only, giving no decoding of specific thoughts.
A seven-hundred-foot tank of two million moving lights matches a volumetric display of many tracked units; Perspecta showed medical anatomy, not a battlefield.
Automata performing card tricks, tightrope walking and fortune telling are performing machines rather than robots serving the public.
Cybernetic governors operating the big wheel in the sky match automatic controllers running a station; the quote does not name onboard computers.
Egg-shaped robots with tractor treads rolling through an opening do not show spoken commands in the quotation.
A mural three-dimensional topographic map flashing on a wall fits a map display, but it shows a relief map, not a volumetric viewable-from-all-sides image.
A broken-down robot sending a distress signal to the nearest unit that helps matches robot coordination, though not a single central computer in the quote.
Reading the Fenachrone's plans from their brains with a mechanical educator matches pulling specific content from a brain; no mechanism is given beyond the device.
Information sent by a mind through helmet pickups to a machine and translated into English matches writing brain content as text; fMRI work showed images, not language.
The line says only that a cold world makes some effect stronger; nothing identifies a brain-reading function in the quotation.
The quote notes a man has four beautiful, tough receptionists and says nothing of voice-operated machines or recognition.
Clerks passing a hidden electronic camera with palms raised matches machine identification of workers for attendance, close to the IBM 357 clocking; it reads a hand, not a card.
A subconscious analysis and mental reactions test points to measuring mind states, but the quote has a gap and no extraction of specific thoughts or images.
A Selector operating on thirty-two kinds of automatic controls matches automated control of a station's functions; the quote does not call it a computer.
An information robot planted in a kiosk on a street matches an automatic answerer of public questions, but the quote does not show language questions or broad knowledge.
Punching buttons on a device that returns cards matched to a person matches a machine selecting from stored records; the whirring wall implies lookup but no search speed.
Gardeners wired to describe and report intruders is robot surveillance with reporting, but the quote does not have them patrol or check credentials as a security robot does.
A stereo projection tank for space and fleet positions matches a three-dimensional display; it is projected on a flat glass wall, not truly volumetric.
A vertical file that is really a robot memory bank matches a machine-stored collection; the quote does not show query matching.
An elevator that delivers a rider on hearing a resident's name matches a machine carrying out a spoken request; the milestone was isolated-word recognition.
Taking language lessons on the way matches machine teaching during idle time, but the quote does not specify sleep or hypnosis.
Metal eyes fixed on a man shows a humanoid robot, but nothing about guarding or checking credentials.
The quote only argues that knowledge needs the Cybers for storage and recall; this is a general statement about retrieval and no details of querying.
A robot responding through an auditory mechanism like an electric eye matches a machine that hears and obeys; the sensor is vague, and the 1972 system was isolated-word.
Casting the thoughts of a person wearing a cap onto a screen for all to see matches displaying mental content visually; the real work reconstructed simple patterns and only after training on scans.
A clerk wiping the information screen and pulling up a scrolling list matches a terminal showing stored records; the nature of the search is not described.
An integrator directory identifying a ship type from generator readings matches a lookup against stored records; the quote shows an answer, not a search.
An Information Center that can answer any question matches a large store answered on demand; humans and video booths imply a service rather than a machine query.
A shipboard Sacred Cow consulted for horoscopes suggests a computer asked questions, but it gives personalized forecasts, not factual answers.
A live human voice answering rather than the usual robot implies robots usually take table calls, an implicit hint at service robots, but no action is shown.
Bringing out the mechanical educator while watching a creature's eyes matches a mind-reading machine used on a person; the quote does not say what it does.
A robot attuned to thought waves that minds a man points to brain-signal control, which is the reverse of reconstructing a thought.
An automatic translating secretary reviewing the agreement matches a machine producing a summary; it records and translates, not listening to dictation.
The quote is only a kit title, The Socialization Kit; nothing indicates a companion robot with romantic or social function.
A robot stating 'I give information' matches a robot attendant answering visitors, though serving customers at tables was the 1985 case.
Slipping an ancient-history tape into a projector shows media playback and not searching a collection for matches.
A red line of caravan points of light gathering into a knot suggests a miniature map display, but nothing indicates volumetric viewing.
Dictating a full account matches a machine receiving dictation; the quote does not say the machine types it.
Whistling the code word so the door opened automatically matches a door opening on a spoken signal; whistling is nonverbal but the voice command function matches.
An arrow shot into a robot's braincase says nothing of a central computer directing robots.
George as a Giant Brain that students and researchers can ask questions in a library matches a computer answering questions; the milestone START answered public English questions.
Individual robot teachers each tapping the central Brain for information match a master computer serving a population of robots; Kalmar carriers were guided, not intelligent.
Questions submitted to a supreme council tower suggests a central store answering any question; the summary's microtapes are not in the quotation.

Automatons demonstrating dress and robot faces showing cosmetic use match robots informing the public as guides; the 1985 robots took restaurant orders.
Reaching for a voicewrite to give a memo matches speaking into a dictation machine; the quote does not say it produces text.
Thought-spectrum experiments that wore out their user are only a reference to experiments, with no display or recorded output stated.
Summoning a mess-robot and selecting dishes matches a robot serving a meal on request, close to a robot waiter; the context is a starship.

Speaking into the microphone of a typing machine that transcribes her words as type matches a voice typing machine; the secretary edits aloud, which fits dictation systems.
